desc:
You must pick some of the given closed intervals [a, b] so that every position in points lies inside at least one picked interval (a point on an end counts as inside). Return the smallest number of intervals you need, or -1 if some point is not inside any interval at all.

points = [1, 5, 9], intervals = [[0, 2], [1, 6], [4, 10], [8, 9]]  ->  2

Picking [1, 6] and [4, 10] covers all three points.
hints: Take the smallest point. Some picked interval must contain it. Which of the intervals containing it is the best choice?

Among the intervals that contain the smallest uncovered point, the one with the largest right end covers the most points further to the right (everything to the left is already covered or is the point itself).

Sort points and intervals. For each point not yet covered, look at all intervals starting at or before it, remember the largest end, check that the end reaches the point (else return -1), count one interval and skip all points up to that end.
editorial: Process the points from left to right. When the current point p is not yet covered, some chosen interval must contain it. Intervals containing p have a ≤ p ≤ b. All points to the left of p are already covered, so only the right end matters, and the interval with the largest b is the best choice: whatever any other candidate covers to the right of p, this one covers too.

Sort the intervals by start and keep a pointer that advances while a ≤ p, maintaining the maximum end best seen so far. Because p only increases, a single pointer suffices and earlier intervals stay available. If best < p, no interval contains p: return -1. Otherwise count one interval and skip every point ≤ best. Total O((n + m) log(n + m)) for the sorts and linear scans after that.
